en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhili of Siming, Song Dynasty.

My late master once resided at Baoyun Monastery and frequently lectured on this scripture; his disciples gathered in great numbers, vying with one another to record what they heard and privately transcribing it onto scrolls.
How much more so when the pen was entrusted to the hands of others—would this not result in a distortion of its vast and profound meaning?
Regarding the intent of this work, its citations from the sutras and śāstras contain many errors and contradictions; each time I encounter the text, I cannot help but feel regret.

Recently, during my lectures, I recalled the essential meanings he had grasped and composed this commentary (*jiwen*). I have further incorporated the secular works and historical records found within *Suyin* (Seeking the Hidden) by Gushan to serve as supplementary aids. It is my hope that readers will not be preoccupied with the external details of the events, but will instead contemplate the benefits of the underlying principles and contemplative insights.
Recorded on the third day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era.
Explanation of the Title, Part Two:
First, the formal title.
The four characters "Jin" (Gold) and so forth are that which is explained (*śeṣya*), while the two characters "wenju" (phrases and sentences) are that which explains (*śeṣaka*).
The title of the sūtra being explained is detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning).
As for the phrases and sentences that explain it: "wen" refers to the sūtra text, and "ju" refers to chapters and sentences, as well as the pauses in recitation (*vireka*).
He then used these chapters and phrases to demarcate the text of the sutra, ensuring that the explanations of its principles each had their own distinct boundaries.
Thus, Jingxi said:
"Because the broad meaning has been fully detailed through the explanation of the title, one need only roughly divide the sections of the sutra text."
The reason the title is called "Wenju" (Textual Explanations) is precisely for this.
However, the establishment of these two characters is merely a mark of humility;
if one examines the commentary on the sutra, its great meanings are by no means few.
Furthermore, the term "text" (wenju) is used as a general designation for all sūtras; therefore, it is distinguished by means of the sūtra's title.
Second is the name of the teacher who expounded it.
The naming of the "abode" (sthāna) is as has been explained previously.

Second, the entry into the text, which has two parts: first, the determination of the three divisions; second, [the detailed explanation]. First, the determination of the three divisions: [two parts]. (Note: The provided text fragment ends here.)
First, regarding the specific identification of the transmitted text:
it differs from the seven fascicles and twenty-two chapters translated by Paramārtha; therefore, it is identified here as consisting of four fascicles and eighteen chapters.

As for those who claim there is a supplementary chapter on "Entrusting" (*parindanā*) making it nineteen chapters, this is an error, because none of the various translated versions contain this chapter.
II. The Correct Judgment of the Three Parts, in two sections:
A. First, citing the judgments of various masters, in two sections:
1. A general presentation of their differences.
"Fullness" refers to advancing; "contraction" refers to retreating.
This speaks of how various masters divide [the land] into three parts, with differing views on advancement and retreat.
Second, under the heading "North of the River," the initial judgment is correctly elucidated in three parts: [The text continues with the three parts.]

First, the masters of the North River [tradition] maintain that because the Four Heavenly Kings each made vows before the Buddha to protect those who preach and listen to the sutra, it is called "the Great Vow Protecting the Sutra";
whereas the Elder Jalavāhana’s curing of illness and saving of fish, and Prince Sattva’s sacrificing his body to feed the tigress, are examples of "Great Compassion Engaging with Sentient Beings."
The intention of this master differs from that of the later and earlier versions of the *Satyasiddhi* [or the *Tattvasiddhi*], yet their general purport is the same.
Second, the masters of Jiangnan:
while their division into three parts is similar to the current one, they were merely unaware that half a chapter of the "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*) belongs to the Introduction (*Nidāna*).
3. Master Paramārtha. This section has two parts: first, the analysis of the text.

During the Liang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha retranslated this sutra, titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra*, adding four chapters: the "Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies," the "Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstacles," the "Chapter on the Dhāraṇī for Purifying the Ground," and the "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows by Relying on Emptiness. These were added to the eighteen chapters of Dharmakṣema’s original version, totaling twenty-two chapters. He then composed a commentary (*śāstra*) to explain it; thus, it is referred to as the "new text" and so forth.
Second, from "The True Meaning" (*Zhendi*) onwards, the meaning is clarified.

It further refutes the [tradition] of Jiangnan, which maintains that the *Jie shouji pin* (Chapter on Bestowing Predictions) and the *Chubing pin* (Chapter on Eliminating Illness) are both currently in circulation; thus it says, "the later [sections on] teacher-disciple, cause, effect, and so forth. [The original text] should have stated "teacher-cause, disciple-effect," as the current wording appears to be inverted.
2. From "Now, the Master" below, the intention of the present Master is shown, in two parts:
first, refuting the various masters based on principle;
second, first, a general censure of human sentiment.
Zheng directly refutes the True Dharma (zhendi), while his meaning also encompasses the region north of the Yangtze River.

According to these two masters, the relationship between teacher and disciple and the sequence of cause and effect are both situated within the orthodox tradition; their intention is that the introductory section (nidāna) has not yet fully distinguished or explained the path of cultivation and realization.

In the section on the Dissemination (Prakīrṇaka), the flavor of the Path has already faded and remains but a mere remnant; therefore, it is refuted in general by stating, "This interpretation is not so.
Second, from "Now, as for the three... onwards, the specific intent of the sutra is demonstrated, in two parts:
first, establishing the position; second... [text continues].
First, the mutual interpenetration of the three divisions is clarified.
"Du" means to block or obstruct.
Since the three divisions together constitute the responsive manifestation of a single scripture, how could their doctrinal principles not mutually encompass one another?
Just as the initial section describes the origination [of the teaching], if it were not present in the latter two sections, how could they be called the "sequence for the correct circulation"?

That which is originated and described within the sequence itself is further proclaimed and disseminated by the section on circulation; otherwise, how could these be termed the "correct exposition" of the entire sutra?
Regarding this section on circulation: if one were to omit the introduction and the main body, through what dharma would it be communicated?
Therefore, each of the three divisions possesses its own three meanings.
The superior, middling, and inferior speech constitutes the excellence of timing (*kālasampad*) among the seven excellences.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that it is "good in the beginning, middle, and end. If it were to be cut off, how could it be called good?
Second, from "Furthermore, the assembly" onwards, it describes the universal benefit for all capacities.

The capacities of those for whom the sutra is intended vary in the speed of their benefit; it is not necessarily the case that all must attain realization within the formal teaching (dharmakāya). Therefore, it is said that their faculties and natures are indeterminate—how could the introductory section (nidāna) possibly be entirely devoid of the flavor of the Dharma?
Is the flavor of the Dharma exhausted and rendered trivial within the section on circulation?
Since this is not the case, what hindrance is there in explaining the cause of Liu-shui (Flowing Water) and the fruit of Hsin-hsiang (Faithful Appearance) within that section on circulation?
"Mi" means "to increase.
"Du" means "to lead.
"Li" means "to exhort."
Second, the section beginning with "Furthermore, another method" cites a scripture.
"The Master" refers to Śākyamuni.

In the "Chapter on Datta," it is explained that in a past kalpa, the Buddha served the Rishi Asita in the body of a king to seek the Mahāyāna Dharma; therefore, this is called the "cause of the Master."
In the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*), the predictions of future buddhahood for Pāśa, Yaśodharā, and others—including their kalpas and lands—constitute the fruit of discipleship.

Ancient Dharma masters, in their commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, judged that everything from the "Chapter on the Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇaka-parivarta*) onwards belongs to the section of Propagation (*Prasaraṇa*), a view universally accepted.

This [text] shares the same intent as the *Jiangnan pian* (Treatise on the South of the River), which currently circulates and contains the karmic relationship between teacher and disciple; thus, it is said that there is no contradiction in meaning.
Nevertheless, one must not adhere to it dogmatically; hence it is said that "bestowal and denial depend upon the person."
2. From "Now" (*jīn*) onwards, according to the meaning, the present section is divided into two parts:

first, the division of the sūtra; second, the determination of the three-part textual structure. Within the first part (the division of the sūtra), there are two sections: first, the determination of the three-part textual structure.

Now, it is divided into three parts, which are largely similar to those of the Jiangnan tradition; however, because the preface occupies nearly half a fascicle, I shall cite the Three Masters [of the North] solely to refute the *Zhendi* (Paramārtha) school.
Second, from "The Preface" onwards, the meaning of the three parts is demonstrated, in two sections:
first, the actual demonstration.
"Jiang" (will) means "shall.

Since the *Zhengzong* (Main Body) and *Liutong* (Circulation) follow the *Xufen* (Introductory Section), the present introduction shall possess the benefit of these two divisions; therefore, it is said that "it will be beneficial."

"Responding precisely to the capacity of the recipient" means it corresponds to the meaning; that is, to precisely address the specific conditions of the recipient, one explains the path of constant fruition through repentance and praise.
"Quan" refers to a fish trap.
A "ji" is a rabbit snare. The fish trap and the rabbit snare serve as metaphors for verbal teachings, while the fish and the rabbit serve as metaphors for the underlying principles and meanings.

Because one wishes to cause these verbal teachings to flow down to future ages—the periods of the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma—and to always enable sentient beings to grasp these principles and meanings, it is said that they shall not be obstructed in future generations.
2. From "The Sūtra says" onwards, the sūtra is cited.
2. From "Those who doubt" onwards, the difficulties are explained, in two parts:
first, the formulation of the objection.

Since it is designated as the "Introductory Section" (*nidāna*), it ought to correspond exactly to the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*); how then could it further include more than half a chapter of the "True Doctrine" (*bhūtanaya*), such as the "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*)?
Second, from "various sūtras" onwards, the general explanation has three parts:
first, citing examples from other sections.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* takes the causes and conditions for the Buddha-land as its primary theme; since it lacks a formal "Introductory Chapter," various masters have taken the first half of the "Buddha-land" chapter to serve as the introductory section.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the "Introductory Chapter" states: "The Buddha, knowing that the assembly had gathered, addressed Śāriputra:

'A bodhisattva who wishes to know all phenomena through the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) should practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*),' and so forth. Such teachings already constitute the main body of the doctrine (*saddharma*), yet they appear within the introductory section (*nidāna*).

If, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, eternal life is taken as the primary theme, and since there is no "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), the gathering of the assembly from within the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) serves as the preface; this refers to the Northern Edition.
If it is the Southern version, Xie Gong edited and finalized it by taking the text on the assembly from the "Life Span" chapter and titling it the "Introduction Chapter.

Regarding these three scriptures, various masters have analyzed them such that either the introduction is included within the main body, or the main body is included within the introduction, without any cause for doubt. How can one alone now doubt the judgment that places the introductory section within the "Life Span" chapter?
2. From "This, moreover," below, the meaning of this sutra is clarified.
This refers to the intention of the compiler regarding the arrangement of the chapters.

Specifically, if the title of the "Chapter on the Lifespan" were placed after the assembly of devas and nāgas in the Hall of Faithful Signs, it would cause the passage concerning the four Buddhas severing doubts to appear abruptly and isolated; hence, it is described as "lofty and distinct."
*Zhan*, pronounced with the *chu* and *xian* finals.
*Zhan* denotes the appearance of a precipitous mountain.
If a character rises in isolation, it is like the perilous and sheer cliffs of a mountain, where there is no continuity or connection.
For this reason, the title "On the Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*) is placed within the introductory section.
Third, from the words "Now, following... onwards, the conclusion is drawn according to the present intention.
Although this chapter belongs to the main body (*bhāga*), its meaning corresponds to the introductory section (*nidāna*). How could one follow the title and thereby cause the meaning to be lost?
Second, from "The Introduction Exists" (*xiu you*) down to the explanation of the three divisions of the scripture:
first, the explanation of the introductory section, which has two parts: [The text continues with the sub-divisions.]
First, the explanation of the title of the chapter, in two parts:
first, the explanation of the introduction, in two parts:
first, the presentation of the three meanings.
The introductory section (*nidāna*) of a sutra, in terms of its meaning, consists of three parts; in some schools, there may be only one or two, which is a matter of omission.
In the present sutra, as well as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other major scriptures, all three are fully present.
2. Below the heading "Next, the Sequence," three meanings are explained.
"Sequence" (xu) refers to the thread-end of a cocoon.
Generally, when drawing silk from a cocoon, one first draws out its sequence; only when the sequence is exhausted does the silk become visible.
Now, these five matters are placed at the beginning like the first strand of a thread.
"Guàn" (冠) is pronounced with a departing tone.

The term "narration" (*xù*) indicates that what is about to be described will provide benefit; specifically, it refers to the benefit of the orthodox transmission and the universal circulation during that time. Therefore, this preface describes the following seventeen chapters.
"Fa" (To issue) means to develop the faith within the capacities of sentient beings.
"Qi" (To arise) means to give rise to the teachings of the Sage's response.

This introduction uses the manifestation of auspicious omens to startle and move the hearts of beings, causing their faith to be expectant and full of longing, so that the teaching will surely provide profound benefit.
Third, "As for the 'Chapter' (*parivarta*)," and below, the explanation of the chapter, which has two parts:
first, citing the Sanskrit and providing the translated name; second, from "The Chapter is...

and below, explaining the meaning based on the name, which has two parts: 1. Citing the Sanskrit and providing the translated name. 2. From "The Chapter is... and below, explaining the meaning based on the name, which has two parts: [The text continues with the sub-divisions.]
First, the formal explanation.
The words and phrases herein are all found in the sūtra.
This is because the teachings that express [the meaning] all employ four factors: namely, sound (*ghoṣa*), names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*).
This is of two kinds:
regarding the characteristics of the Buddha’s voice during his lifetime—namely, the eight tones and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) in the Brahma-voice—one is real;

whereas the collections of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and syllables (*vyañjanakāya*) are merely provisional constructs established upon the modulations of sound, and these three are thus conventional.

Sound belongs to the category of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); while the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) belong to the third aggregate, the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Regarding these, there are differences in the positions established by the two schools—the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna—as seen in the *Abhidharmapada* (14), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (17), and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (24).

Regarding names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*): the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, "Names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); phrases express distinctions (*viśeṣa*); syllables are the characters (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for these two."

If we consider the collections made by the various noble ones after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—whether the palm-leaf manuscripts of that land or the yellow scrolls of this region—the names, phrases, and sentences contained therein are all established based on the physical forms and appearances of color-dharmas.
Now, these two have been briefly cited; in full, they should comprise four.

As for "those of similar category following one another": for instance, because four dharmas equally clarify the meaning of "initiation" and so forth, they are divided into the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*); and so on, up to where they equally clarify the meaning of "praising the Buddha," they are divided into the "Chapter of Praise" (*Stuti-parivarta*).
Although the introduction has now been explained, the meaning of the chapters extends throughout the following sections.
Second, citing examples:

the textual phrasing and stylistic categories of both the Vinaya and Abhidharma Piṭakas possess divisions such as *varga*, *skandhaka*, and *khaṇḍa*, which correspond to the *varga* (chapters) of the Sūtras.
Regarding the "sections and groups" (piānjù), this refers to the five sections and six groups:
first, pārājika; second, saṃghāvaśeṣa; third, pāyattika; fourth, prātideśanīya; and fifth, duṣkṛta. These are called the five sections.
If *sthalāntika* (grave offenses) are added below the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offenses requiring suspension), they are called the six groups (*ṣaṭ-nikāya*).
If, further, *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) are expanded to include "evil speech," they become seven groups.
Regarding *Abhidharma*: the full term is *Abhidharma*, which here means "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*); it refers to the *Śāstra-piṭaka* (the Abhidharma Piṭaka).
*Kaṇḍa* (犍度) means "collection of dharmas" (*dharmaskandha*); it refers to a single section consisting of a collection of dharmas that follow one another according to their common characteristics.
For example, the *Aṣṭaka-kaṇḍa-śāstra* (八犍度論) consists of: first, the *Karma-kaṇḍa*, which elucidates the three types of karma;
and second, the *Anuśaya-kaṇḍa*, which elucidates the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
The three knowledges, four concentrations, five faculties, six elements, seven views, and eight miscellaneous items can be understood by reflecting upon them.
Second, from "As it is" (*tathatā*) onwards, the commentary on the sūtra text has two parts:
first, the division into three prefaces.
Although this is divided into three parts, when reaching the subsequent section on the commentary, they are condensed into two: the general introduction and the specific introduction.
Second, the explanation of the three introductions has three parts:
first, the explanation of their sequence, which has two parts: [1a]...
First, a general discussion of names and numbers, in two parts:
first, clarifying that the numbers differ, in two parts;
first, the actual clarification of the opening and closing of the numbers.
The "Dishen" (Earth-Person) refers to the masters who propagated the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).

Regarding the "six matters": first, the essence of the Dharma heard; second, the person capable of upholding it; third, the harmony between hearing and upholding; fourth, the teaching master; fifth, the place of reliance; and sixth, the companions for hearing and upholding.
If there are seven, one is separated from "I have heard.
If there are five, one is united with the Buddha's dwelling.
Second, it simultaneously demonstrates the right and wrong of the assembly.
Since this sutra primarily discusses the doctrine of eternal life within the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, the devas, nāgas, and bodhisattvas have gathered here to listen.
Once the preaching is concluded, the four Buddhas do not appear; it is therefore logical that the assembly should withdraw and disperse.
The introduction to the *Lingshan* [sermon] and the golden drum in the dream differ in both time and place; therefore, [the former audience] did not hear it.

Based on the principle that those who have attained the lifespan of the eternal hearing are considered "co-hearers," those who were not present for the dream and so forth are not considered co-hearers.
Because the time and place at which this sutra was preached are not fixed, the assembly of those who heard it together does not follow the sequential arrangement found in other sutras.
If one examines Yijing’s new translation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, the listing of the assembly of those who heard it together does not differ from that of other sutras.
The Great Master, knowing in advance that the Sanskrit original was about to arrive, therefore provided these annotations.
Second, regarding the various names established below the phrase "This [text]": this section has two parts;
first, the listing and explanation of alternative names.
There are six titles in total; in each case, the preceding phrase provides the name and the subsequent phrase explains its meaning.
Regarding the "Seal of Definition" (mudrā-niyama): by means of such phrases, it is like a worldly seal or signature; seeing them at the beginning of a text, one knows it to be a Buddha-sūtra.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "It is not only my own teaching that is thus; the sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time likewise begin in this manner.
To serve as the basis for the general designation [of "sūtra"], everything spoken from the Golden Mouth is prefaced with these words; therefore, they are collectively termed "sūtras" (*jing*).
The "Postscript to the Sūtra" (Sūtra-paścāt-nidāna) is so called because it was compiled after the preaching of the sūtra.
The "Prologue to the Sūtra" (Sūtra-pūrva-nidāna) is so called because the Buddha’s final injunction directed that it be placed at the beginning of the sūtra.
The *Mahā-śāstra* states: "When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, Ānanda asked the Buddha:"
"What words should be placed at the beginning of all sutras?
The Buddha answered Ānanda:
"One should say: 'Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a region, in such-and-such a country, together with such-and-such a great assembly.'"
Regarding the "Preface to the Refutation of Heresy": all non-Buddhist scriptures are headed by the two characters *ā* and *u*.

*Ā* signifies "non-existence" (*abhāva*) and *u* signifies "existence" (*bhāva*). Because these [heretics] take these two as their fundamental basis, nothing within their various schools transcends existence and non-existence; therefore, [the author] establishes this [work] to refute such false attachments, showing them to be neither correct nor valid.
Regarding the "Certification of Faith" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upodghāta), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Why not speak directly of Prajñā, rather than speaking of dwelling in Rājagṛha?
Answer:
To cause people to have faith by specifying the time, place, and persons."
2. "Tiantai" and below conclude by returning to the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the Master Tiantai, Zhanran refers to the Venerable Zhizhe as the "Master Tiantai" in contrast to the older interpretations of that school.
Regarding the four *siddhāntas*: *siddha* is a term from the Hu-language (Sanskrit), meaning "pervasive.
*Tān* is a Sanskrit word, which here is translated as "bestowal" (*dāna*).

The Buddhas and sages constantly bestow upon sentient beings the four kinds of benefits—joy, the generation of goodness, the destruction of evil, and entry into principle—in a manner that is all-pervasive; this is the general characteristic of responsive resonance.
This sequence being established by the Golden Mouth is the "response" (ying).
That all subsequent conditions and opportunities are extinguished is the "stimulus" (gan).
Now, regarding this single sequence which possesses six names and meanings, what is their significance?
Now, if these are subsumed under the four *siddhāntas*, then each name and meaning finds its proper place of return.

Thus, the first two pairs of names pertain to the world and are bestowed upon sentient beings for their benefit; the third and fourth names belong to the "for-the-sake-of-others" (*puruṣakāra*); the fifth, which refutes the heterodox, is the remedial method (*prātipakṣika*); and the sixth, which trusts in principle, belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Since these four have not yet been distinguished by depth or shallowness, each of the four teachings must possess all four [aspects].
Second, under "The Old Explanation," the text provides a formal commentary on the sūtra in two parts:
first, an explanation of the five meanings based on the sūtra; second, [the subsequent section].
Second, the explanation of the meaning of the omission of the "those who heard together" (saha-śruta).
This is because the masters of the *Dilun* school divide the text into six categories;
however, according to the five categories, there are currently only four [categories] in the extant text.
Regarding the first [section], there are five parts:
first, the explanation of the essence of the Dharma, which has two sub-sections;
first, the ancient interpretation, which has two further parts: [1a]...
First, the citation of the interpretations of various masters, which has four parts:
first, the ancient interpretation; second, Master Zhaos; third, Paramārtha; and fourth, Nāgārjuna.
The textual meaning of these four is all clearly visible, yet it is only upon reaching the judgment of the four *siddhāntas* that their relative depth or shallowness can be definitively established.
Second, from "This... onwards, the text judges [the teaching] by means of the four *siddhāntas*.

It is now clarified that whether the sacred Dharma is extensive or concise, general or specific, there is nothing that is not a response to an invocation; such responses do not transcend the four kinds of *siddhānta*.
The previous judgment concerning the names and meanings of the six categories was general and comprehensive;
the present judgment concerning the individual responses and inducements of each of the six matters is specific and particular.
Therefore, the two characters "thus" (rú shì) have been interpreted differently by various masters.

Today, the Tiantai masters interpret this through the four *siddhāntas*, each capturing the single intent of the Tathāgata’s responsive manifestation; how could they be like those who argue in the world that one is right while all others are wrong?

Although the interpretation of these two characters [in the older commentary] accords with the textual structure, it fails to distinguish between the great and the small, as its terminology is general and lacks the characteristics of the three benefits of generating goodness; it merely achieves the benefit of ensuring that the transmission of the teaching is not erroneous, and thus belongs to the mundane level (*loka*).

Although Master Zhao possesses words that accord with principle, he does not distinguish between the ultimate and the conventional; rather, he merely gives rise to faith and compliance through his innate goodness, and thus his work belongs to the category of "benefiting humans.

Furthermore, while the textual patterns of the *Zhendi* (Ultimate Truth) do not yet differentiate [between the two truths], its treatise definitively eliminates the faults of exaggeration and depreciation, and thus it constitutes "remedial therapy" (*pratipakṣa*).

Although Nāgārjuna’s faith and compliance were the same as those of Master Sengzhao, his statement that "this matter is thus" (shì shì rúshì) serves to manifest the meaning of the three truths: "this matter" (shì shì) is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), "thus" (rú) is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and "is" (shì) is the middle truth (madhyama-satya).

This skillfully demonstrates the three truths within a single phrase; it corresponds to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Regarding the note "and so forth," it means to explain as previously argued. Second, from "Now I shall... onwards, the current explanation has two parts: 1. The title. 2. The main body of the explanation. This has two parts: A. An overview. B. A detailed exposition. This has two parts: i. Refuting the heterodox views of others. ii. Establishing the correct principle. This has two parts: (a) Briefly stating the thesis. (b) Extensively explaining the meaning. This has two parts: 1. Explaining the first verse. This has two parts: a. Briefly stating the thesis. b. Extensively explaining the meaning. This has two parts: i. Refuting the heterodox views of others. This has two parts: (a) Refuting the view that the nature of reality is non-existent. (b) Refuting the view that the nature of reality is existent. ii. Establishing the correct principle. This has two parts: (a) Establishing the correct principle regarding the non-existence of the nature of reality. These two interpretations discuss the dual excellence of both teaching and contemplation, standing far above all other schools; this is due to their merit.
The first section of the text is divided into two parts:
first, the general [explanation].
Regarding this, the nature of suchness (*tathatā*) is clarified through both the teaching and the transmission; its being so (*tathatva*) is clarified through both the practice and the reception.

Since this constitutes a general explanation, it must encompass all four teachings throughout the subsequent specific explanations; thus, we know that the "Dharma-characteristics" (dharmalakṣaṇa) are what is expounded by the four [teachings], the Buddha is the master who proclaims the four teachings, and Ānanda is the person who hears and upholds the four. Speaking from the perspective of their respective divisions, all four are as vast as the great ocean.
2. Detailed Explanation, in three parts:
First, alternating explanations of refutation and establishment, in four sections.
That is to say, each of the four teachings successively refutes the "not so" and "not thus" of the preceding ones, before establishing the meaning of its own teaching as being "thus."
First, refuting the heterodox and establishing the orthodox.
This consists of two parts: first, refuting the heterodox; second, revealing the orthodox of the Tripiṭaka.
Regarding the first, refuting the heterodox:
Regarding the term "Āṅ" as auspicious, the *Śata-śāstra* clarifies that when an outsider asked an inner disciple,
"What Dharma does the Buddha teach?
the answer was given as follows:
"In brief, there are two kinds:
the cessation of evil and the practice of good.
The outsider asked:
"Your scripture contains a fault; because it speaks of evil at the beginning, it is inauspicious.
The scriptures and teachings of my Master speak of auspiciousness at the beginning.

For instance, in the *Gṛhapati-vistara-sūtra* and others, all begin by saying "Auspicious. Because they are auspicious at the beginning, they are also auspicious in the middle and at the end; therefore, the word *āyuṣmat* (long-lived) signifies auspiciousness.
Regarding the phrase "the text is inconsistent" (*wen guai*): using the correct to refute the false is not the same as being incorrect.

Although the scripture initially designates what is auspicious, the content explained within the section consists solely of false views; thus, this text is inconsistent with principle and is not "like" (proper).
Heterodox views are inauspicious; how could they be called *āyu*?
This principle differs from the literal text and is therefore incorrect.
Thus, the *Śata-śāstra* refutes this, stating: "To say 'this is auspicious' or 'this is inauspicious' is the breath of heterodox views."
Second, from "The text is like" (*wen ru*) onwards, the correct position is established.

In the Tripitaka teaching, the text and the principle correspond to one another; because the discourse on impermanence and arising-and-ceasing accords with the principle of impermanence and arising-and-ceasing, it is called "like" (*ru*); because this principle accords with the text, it is called "is" (*shi*).
2. From "Now it is said" below, there is the refutation of difference and the establishment of identity, in two parts:
first, the refutation of difference.
To manifest the principle of the Mahāyāna, one first repudiates the errors of the Hīnayāna.
The conventional, which exists as a reality and serves as the expressive signifier, does not coincide with the ultimate truth; therefore, it is not "as-it-is.
The ultimate truth, which is the signified, does not encompass the principle of the Middle Way; because it is shallow, it is not [the final state].
Second, the section below "Mo" (摩) clarifies their commonality.
Universally speaking, illusory existence is emptiness in its very essence; this non-differentiation is termed "Suchness.
This true emptiness is capable of containing the Middle Way, which differs from the shallow analytical emptiness of the Tripiṭaka [teachings]; therefore, the principle is correctly named.
The Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) necessarily encompasses both the Distinct (Biejiao) and Complete (Yuanjiao) Teachings; therefore, the text designates it as the Mahāyāna.
Third, from "Now, regarding the three" onwards, there is the refutation of the shallow to clarify the profound, in two parts:
first, the refutation of the shallow.
To clarify the distinct principle, one must first refute the common [teaching].

In the Common Teaching, the three vehicles hear equally that all is empty; yet, those of dull faculties among the bodhisattvas understand it in the same way as the two vehicles, while those of sharp faculties, upon hearing of emptiness, do not merely realize the emptiness of existence but are also able to realize the emptiness of emptiness itself.
Since these are each understood individually, they do not accord with the distinct [teachings];
as for the two proofs regarding emptiness, those proofs of emptiness are even more inferior, and thus cannot be compared to the [teaching of] the Middle Way.
Second, clarifying its profundity.

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) does not extend to the study and practice of the Two Vehicles; although it broadly encompasses a multitude as numerous as motes of dust, it is exclusively for those with the faculties of Bodhisattvas, all of whom hear of Buddha-nature and enter its cultivation through a sequential process.
Since there is no divergent interpretation, it is called "as-it-is" (*tathatā*);
since there is nothing that does not realize the Middle, it is called "correct" (*bhūta*).
Fourth, from "Now, [I] say 'detached'" below, the refutation of the establishment of the Middle by means of detachment has two parts:
First, the refutation of separation.
To clarify the principle of perfection, one must first repudiate the errors of partiality.

Although the partial teachings speak of the "Middle," that Middle pertains only to the Buddha-realm; even though they transform and create the causes and effects of the nine realms, those nine are not inherently possessed (*xingju*). One must therefore rely on the Middle Way to gradually sever and exhaust [defilements] before finally attaining the Buddha-realm.
Because the Buddha differs from these nine [views], they are not called "suchness" (tathatā).

First, one contemplates transcending the mundane; next, one contemplates transcending the conventional truth; reaching the third contemplation, one simultaneously transcends both truths and realizes the Middle Way. Since the Middle is not identical to the extremes, this [interpretation] is not the correct meaning.
Second, from the section on "Characters" (*akṣara*) below, the Middle Way is clarified.
The characters that express [the truth] are by nature originally forgotten and detached; they do not differ from the principle, and are therefore called "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
They are merely emptiness, merely existence, merely form, and merely mind; each and every one is the Middle Way, none of which is not the Buddha-dharma, and is therefore called "This."
The phrasing accords with principle, and the meaning is ultimately established.
Second, from "First, the refutation" onwards, the four teachings are summarized and established.
Question:
In the previous explanation of the four teachings, the Profound Principle was named because it encompassed both the True and the Middle;
now, in concluding the discussion of the four teachings, it is said that the Separate Teaching "breaks the shallow to clarify the profound.
How could it be that both the True and the Middle of the Shared Teaching are shallow?
Answer:
Although the universal principle is profound, it incorporates both shallow and profound principles in order to encompass those of the two vehicles and the dull-witted bodhisattvas.

Now, concluding with the distinct teaching (*biejiao*), which is exclusively for bodhisattvas and discusses only the profound principle, one uses "only the profound" to refute "incorporating the shallow"; thus, this does not contradict the previous explanation of the meaning.
Third, from "This sutra" onwards, it is shown that the section possesses the four [aspects].
Second, Contemplating the Mind:

One contemplates the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth by means of the perfect threefold contemplation; the mind that cultivates evil is itself the inherent evil nature, termed the "evil dharma-realm," wherein no phenomenon is not subsumed.
Its substance consists of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), which are also termed the three truths (*tri-satya*).
When these are designated as truths and illuminated, the object of contemplation is not distinct from the contemplation itself;

therefore, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*). As for the statement that "the object is identical to correct contemplation": the object is original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), while its arising is initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). Although they are distinguished as new and old, the essence of enlightenment does not differ; thus, it is appropriately said that the object is identical to correct contemplation, and this meaning is thereby established.
If it were not so, how could the four propositions—such as "the object illuminating the object"—be established?

When the Sūtra uses the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), if one contemplates an insentient object with a mind that is biased, narrow, or forgetful, and falsely establishes it as *tathatā* (Suchness) and the like, all such instances are termed "erroneous contemplation."

Although this current "Correct Contemplation" (zhèngguān) is not a summary of practice, if a practitioner wishes to integrate phenomena into principle and cultivate according to what they have heard, they must distinguish the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*) within the mind that is the object of contemplation: the aggregate-object (*skandha-viṣaya*) is constantly present, while the remaining nine await their arousal.

Regarding the contemplation of that which can be contemplated, one must recognize the ten vehicles: those of superior capacity cultivate one; those of middling capacity proceed up to seven; and those of inferior capacity complete all seven.

If you yourself do not yet understand the *Mohe zhiguan*, you should consult with teachers and friends on each point individually; only after clearly identifying the medicine and the illness should you practice it. Do not think that practicing a single phrase is sufficient.
The subsequent exegesis and interpretation should be understood according to this principle.
Second, from "Thus have I heard" onwards, the explanation of hearing and upholding has two parts: first, the traditional (or old) interpretation, which has three sub-sections:
[The text continues with the specific points of the traditional interpretation.]
First, regarding the former masters:
because externalists hold views of a self, they mostly claim "I am the teacher"; Ānanda, however, took the Buddha as his teacher, and thus he proclaimed, "I have heard.
Second, regarding ultimate truth.
Because I am able to receive and uphold the Dharma taught by the Buddha, this constitutes the meaning of being a "vessel.
By excluding those who are not vessels, the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) are revealed and established.
Although the distinctions between the wisdoms of the four teachings have not yet been analyzed, this interpretation of "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) far surpasses previous explanations.
Third, the *Śikṣāsamuccaya-bhāṣya*.
That work explains that auditory consciousness arises from four conditions: first, space; second, the sense organ; third, the object; and fourth, attention (*manasikāra*).

The present text states that "the unimpaired" refers to the sense organ, "a place where sound can be heard" refers to the object, and "listening attentively" refers to attention; thus, it is only deficient in the condition of space.
The subsequent statement, "the harmony of causes and conditions," can encompass both meanings.
That is to say, it is only through the harmony of the four conditions that auditory consciousness arises.
The reason it does not say "the ear hears" but rather "I hear" is that "I" is the master of the ear.
The new [school] says that the ear-consciousness arises from nine conditions; this is fully detailed in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Second, regarding the "Master’s Explanation" below, the current explanation has two parts:
first, the explanation according to the teachings, which has two sub-parts: [The text continues with the second sub-part.]
First, the individual explanations of "I hear" (evam mayā śrutam) have two parts.
First, the clarification of the four types of "self.
These instances of "I" and "myself" are established by analogy with the four phrases—such as "birth after birth" (*jāti-jāti*) and so forth—found in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
However, this "self" (*ātman*) is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), existing by appropriating the aggregates (*skandha*).
Since the phenomena of the aggregates possess the four characteristics such as arising and so forth, how could it not be the case that the self likewise follows these real dharmas?

As the commentary on "the arising of arising" states: "The great arising gives rise to the small arising. This means that arising-and-ceasing gives rise to arising-and-ceasing; one appropriates the dharma of arising-and-ceasing to constitute a self of arising-and-ceasing. Therefore, by analogy, the arising of arising produces the self of the self.
Although this is the contemplation of emptiness, it is not the realization of emptiness as the essence; therefore, the Tripitaka belongs to the first category.

Furthermore, one should know that while the conventional and the real, and arising and ceasing, are the very nature of sentient beings, they do not realize it; now, by receiving this teaching, they contemplate in accordance with that fundamental nature.
Is this true only for this teaching?
It is so for all three lower teachings as well.
In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), real dharmas arise and yet do not arise; thus, the self within the aggregates is precisely non-self, and therefore it belongs to the second phrase.
Others perceive that the aggregates (skandhas) do not arise yet they arise; therefore, they contemplate non-self (*anātman*) as self.

It is because of this teaching that one first knows the true self (*ātman*); however, since pride (*māna*) is prevalent, one first contemplates non-self, next refutes non-self, establishes the self, and finally enters the true self. Therefore, this teaching corresponds to the third stage.

The person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) immediately realizes that the provisional and the real before one are neither-arising-nor-non-arising; by gathering the eternally abiding aggregates (skandhas), they constitute the true self.

Since this self is itself the Middle Way, both truths converge therein. Thus it is said that "self and non-self are non-dual" regarding the meaning of the true self. For this reason, this teaching corresponds to the fourth phrase.

The teaching is fundamentally intended for those with specific capacities; therefore, the doctrine of the four types of self is correlated with the four root-natures (indriya) so that later exponents may analyze them as described above—hence the note "and so forth.
Second, the clarification of the four types of hearing.
"I" am the subject of hearing, and "hearing" is my function; the subject is a provisional person, while the function is a real dharma.
However, if one understands the meaning of "arising," then the meaning of "hearing" will manifest of itself.

"Birth" (jāti) is a general discussion of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), whereas "hearing" (śruta) refers specifically to the act of listening; thus, there is a slight difference between them.
Because further hearing arises from the causal condition of hearing, it is called "hearing-hearing" (*śruta-śruta*).
Since it arises from conditions, it ultimately returns to destruction; this is hearing arising and ceasing.
Hearing has no four natures, and in its own place there is no hearing; therefore it is called "hearing and not hearing"—this is hearing without arising.
Although in truth there is no hearing, within the conventional there is hearing; therefore it is called "hearing that which is not heard," meaning this hearing is immeasurable.
Because the two truths are themselves the Middle Way, it is said "not heard";
yet since the Middle Way itself cannot be apprehended, it is further said "not heard."
For forty-nine years he did not utter a single word; how could there be a center or periphery to be heard?
This hearing is non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Pay attention as before.
2. From "There are four" onwards, my hearing [of the Dharma] is explained together with its commentary in three parts:
first, the four capacities of the hearer.
Within the Tripiṭaka teaching, Ānanda possesses four virtues within a single body, and thus receives four names.
The *Āgama* was produced from the *Zangdian* (Treasury of the Canon), while the other three were produced from the *Zhengfa nian* (*Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Now, in expounding these minor names in relation to the Four Teachings, the meaning accords with the name.
"Ānanda" is the term in the Sanskrit language; "Joyful One" (Huanxi) is its meaning in the vernacular.
He was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment, and the entire nation rejoiced; thus he was named accordingly.
Since his name was established based on these conditions, it accords with the law of arising and ceasing. As he is to transmit and uphold the Tripitaka, it is appropriate that he use this name."

In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the essence and phenomena are taught as being identical to principle; since this differs from the views of ordinary people, it is appropriate to use the title "Worthy" (*xian*).

In the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), the five periods discuss the Buddha-dharma as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, encompassing many areas of mastery; thus, it is appropriate to use the title "Keeper of the Treasury" (*zangdian*).
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) elucidates the principle of the Dharma-realm from beginning to end; as it is both profound and vast, it is appropriate to employ the name of the ocean.
Second, "Joyful" and below, refers to those capable of upholding the four Buddhas, which has four parts.
First, the Tripitaka.
This teaching analyzes phenomena (dharmas) and its emptiness does not include the "middle"; therefore, the vision of the Buddha’s body is only that of the sixteen-foot form.
Second, from "Xian-a" [xian-ā] onwards is the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Having contemplated and realized the nature of phenomena, one manifests two kinds of emptiness, namely: the "limited" (but) and the "unlimited" (not-but).

Bodhisattvas of dull faculties, like those of the Two Vehicles, perceive only limited emptiness; because they lack the realization of the central reality, this [emptiness] is not the fundamental nature of form and mind.

Therefore, because the Buddha has fundamentally eliminated all residual habits through his vows, his manifested body and wisdom ultimately return to extinction like ashes; yet, because his physical form has a defined dimension, it is said to be sixteen feet tall.

For bodhisattvas of sharp faculties who receive the distinct or perfect teachings, they understand that this is not merely emptiness, but that emptiness is the true, substantial essence of original enlightenment. This is the wondrous form-mind realized at the stage of Buddhahood; its manifest body and wisdom accord with that essence and are boundless. Thus, it is called the "Distinguished Body" (Zhuntè)—venerable, sublime, and extraordinary—and is also termed the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body).
There is but one Buddha-body; however, because it appears in two forms according to the sharp or dull faculties of sentient beings, it is called the "unified body" (he-shen).
This distinction must be made regarding the Buddha-body in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

One should understand that when those of dull faculties perceive the Buddha—even if he is ten li high, or even a hundred billion li high—because they rely on mere emptiness, this is not the Honored Unique Body (zunte), for it remains limited by spatial boundaries.

If those who benefit from the teaching see [the Buddha] as sixteen or eight feet tall, this is already based on the Middle Way and thus lacks fixed dimensions; for this reason, the *Wenju* explains that the verses of praise for the thirty-two marks by King Suvarṇanāga in the following section are precisely extolling the *viśeṣa-buddha-kāya* (the sublime, extraordinary body).
III. Below "The Canon" (Dian) is the Separate Teaching (Biejiao).

In this teaching, those at the initial stage of the path immediately hear of the "Middle Only" (danzhong). Although this Middle does not fully encompass the nine realms of existence—including their environments and inhabitants—it is not devoid of the wondrous form and mind of the Buddha-realm. Therefore, the vision of the Buddha consists solely of the majestic and distinctive body (zunteshen) that is without spatial limitation.
This is because this teaching, from beginning to end, is not shared with the two vehicles or with bodhisattvas dwelling in emptiness regarding its cultivation and realization.
Fourth, "Sea" and below refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Since this teaching explains that the characteristics of the world are eternal, all phenomena are none other than the Middle Way.

Although others may likewise perceive the *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa* (excellent marks), they do so through combined distinct cultivation, whereas here [in our teaching], these are all intrinsically complete (*prakṛti-pariniṣpanna*). Thus, the Dragon Girl said:
"The subtle and pure Dharma-body is endowed with the thirty-two marks."
To manifest the perfection of its nature, it is therefore designated preeminently as the *dharmakāya*.

Thus, this teaching instructs people to contemplate the suffering and joy inherent in the virtues of nature, thereby giving rise to the resolve to provide succor and deliverance; for it takes the very poisons that afflict reason as that which is to be subjugated and eliminated. The three causes of cultivated virtue are termed the "virtues of nature," while the two bodies—the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*—are themselves termed the *dharmakāya*.

This is because one seeks to dissolve cultivation within the nature itself: suffering is uprooted without being uprooted, poison is neutralized without being neutralized, practice is cultivated without being cultivated, and Buddhahood is realized without being realized.
Ānanda transmitted these Unconditioned Four Truths; this is teaching through non-teaching. Therefore, he was one who personally received [the Dharma] from the Dharmakāya Buddha.
Third, below the word "this," there are four types of capacities within the section.
Question:
Above, the four teachings were clarified; why now do you speak only of the three vehicles in terms of preaching and listening?
Answer:
Within the Three Vehicles, for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one must discuss the Tripitaka and the Shared Teaching; if one clarifies the Bodhisattva path, one must encompass all four teachings.

While the Three Vehicles are discussed collectively, the four teachings are distinguished individually. Since the listeners belong to the Three Vehicles, the speaker must necessarily be the Four Buddhas;
since each understands according to their own voice, they likewise perceive differently from a single body.
The previous explanation of the "unification of the body" (合身) has this meaning in mind.
Second, from "Contemplation" (觀) onwards, the explanation is given in terms of the contemplative mind (*citta*).
Thus far, the fourfold meanings of "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) have been analyzed according to the practitioner’s mental contemplation.
"Climbing to the superior" refers to the sixfold contemplation (*ṣaḍākāra-bhāvanā*) of the contaminated dhyānas (*sāsrava-dhyāna*).

One contemplates the "purity, excellence, and detachment" of the higher stage while feeling "aversion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obstruction" of the lower stage; this is discussed in terms of "upper" and "lower" across the nine stages (*navabhūmi*).

"I" and "I hear" refer to the arising and ceasing of conventional objects within the Tripitaka. The former section concerned the entry into principle through the contemplation of arising and ceasing based on the understanding of the Three Vehicles; the present section concerns how ordinary persons, practicing without such knowledge, achieve only mundane dhyāna.

Since this is the conventional realm (*saṃvṛti*), whether one knows it or not, phenomena are fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing; therefore, it corresponds to the phrase "arising and arising.

Now, our school explains this: whether from the perspective of the capacities of those to be converted, or by way of the contemplation of the subject who contemplates, the two types of contemplation—the analytical and the contemplation of essence—distinguish the conventional as different while recognizing the ultimate as identical.
Previously, based on conventional differences, the analysis of phenomena was matched individually against the first phrase;
now, proceeding from ultimate identity, the analysis of their substance is matched collectively against the second phrase. The latter two contemplations do not differ from the preceding pairings.

Furthermore, while the previous discussion regarding the teachings could apply the four phrases of "I have heard" to four different types of people, the present discourse on the cultivation of contemplation must be understood in terms of a single person’s single moment of thought.

Thus, the *Shiqian* states that within the threefold contemplation of one mind, one perceives the four sets of the Four Truths within a single thought-moment; since this already encompasses the four realms of existence (*gati*), how could it possibly lack the mundane meditative concentrations?
Therefore, it is said that there must be a sequence, as the characteristics are distinguished according to the person;
yet in practice there is no before or after, for one achieves only the perfect contemplation.
Third, from "at one time" onwards, the harmony and integration is clarified, in two parts:
First, the ancient interpretations, in two parts:
first, Master Zhaol.
"Qi" means to open.

Second, regarding the section beginning with "The Three Baskets," there are two parts concerning Paramārtha: 1. The title and the translator's name. 2. The preface to the translation. First, the title and the translator's name: *The Commentary on the Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha. Second, the preface to the translation: The *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra* was composed by the Bodhisattva Asaṅga. Its purpose is to explain the profound meaning of the Mahāyāna and to refute the heterodox views of the Śrāvakas and others. It consists of ten fascicles and contains five hundred verses. It is divided into eight chapters: the Chapter on the Nature of the Dharma, the Chapter on the Meaning of the Dharma, the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Dharma, the Chapter on the Practice of the Dharma, the Chapter on the Obstacles to the Dharma, the Chapter on the Purification of the Dharma, the Chapter on the Attainment of the Dharma, and the Chapter on the Manifestation of the Dharma. Each chapter has its own specific meaning, yet they all converge upon the single principle of the Mahāyāna. Paramārtha, whose courtesy name was Zhendi, was a native of Ujjayinī in Western India. He was a descendant of the Ikṣvāku clan and a direct heir to the Buddha’s lineage. He arrived in the Liang capital during the Tianjian era. During the Datong era of the Chen dynasty, he was summoned to the capital. He resided at the Hongfu Monastery and translated numerous scriptures, including the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra*. His translations were characterized by their adherence to the original Sanskrit meanings and his mastery of both the source language and the vernacular. He passed away in the seventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty at the age of seventy-seven. Regarding this treatise: when the Great Master Tanyan first encountered it, he was struck by its profundity and requested that it be translated. However, the text was difficult to understand, and the translation remained incomplete. Later, the Great Master Jizang, hearing of its existence, sought it out with great effort. He obtained the manuscript from the monk Huikai and, with the assistance of the monk Daoyuan, finally completed the translation. This work is essential for those who wish to penetrate the ultimate truth of the Mahāyāna. It is not merely a commentary on the words; it reveals the underlying intent of the Buddha’s teaching. Therefore, one must study it with utmost diligence. [End of Preface] Third, the body of the treatise: The first chapter is the Chapter on the Nature of the Dharma. It explains that the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally pure and identical to the nature of the Tathāgata. It refutes the views of those who hold that the self is eternal or that all things are annihilated after death. It establishes that the true nature of reality is beyond conceptualization and linguistic expression, yet it can be realized through the wisdom of non-discrimination. This nature is neither existent nor non-existent; it is the middle way that transcends all extremes. By understanding this, one abandons the afflictions of grasping and attains liberation. [End of First Chapter] Fourth, the second part of the commentary: The second chapter is the Chapter on the Meaning of the Dharma. It explains that the meaning of the Mahāyāna is vast and inconceivable. It distinguishes between the provisional teachings given to those of inferior capacity and the definitive teachings intended for those of superior capacity. It clarifies that the ultimate goal of all Buddhas is to lead sentient beings to the state of Buddhahood. Furthermore, it discusses the three bodies of the Buddha—the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya—and how these manifest in accordance with the capacities of beings. It emphasizes that while the manifestations may differ, the underlying essence remains one and the same. This chapter serves to dispel doubts and provide a clear understanding of the Mahāyāna path. [End of Second Chapter] Fifth, the third part of the commentary: The third chapter is the Chapter on the Characteristics of the Dharma. It examines the various characteristics of phenomena as they appear in the world. It explains that although phenomena arise and perish according to causes and conditions, their true nature remains unchanging. It uses analogies such as water and waves to illustrate how the mind gives rise to the appearance of objects. It warns against clinging to these appearances as real, for such clinging leads to suffering. Instead, one should cultivate wisdom to see through the illusory nature of phenomena and realize the emptiness of all dharmas. [End of Third Chapter] Sixth, the fourth part of the commentary: The fourth chapter is the Chapter on the Practice of the Dharma. It outlines the stages of practice required to realize the Mahāyāna. It begins with the cultivation of faith and proceeds through the development of wisdom, compassion, and skillful means. It describes the perfections (pāramitās) and the bodhisattva stages (bhūmis). It emphasizes that practice must be grounded in both wisdom and compassion; otherwise, one falls into the extremes of either nihilism or eternalism. Through diligent practice, one gradually purifies the mind and advances toward the attainment of Buddhahood. [End of Fourth Chapter] Seventh, the fifth part of the commentary: The fifth chapter is the Chapter on the Obstacles to the Dharma. It identifies the various obstacles that hinder progress on the path. These include the obstacles of afflictions, the obstacles of karma, and the obstacles of ignorance. It explains how each of these functions to obscure the true nature of reality. It provides methods for overcoming these obstacles, such as the cultivation of the four immeasurables (brahmavihāras) to counteract hatred, the practice of generosity to counteract greed, and the application of analytical wisdom to counteract ignorance. By removing these hindrances, the practitioner gains clarity and advances toward enlightenment. [End of Fifth Chapter] Eighth, the sixth part of the commentary: The sixth chapter is the Chapter on the Purification of the Dharma. It describes the process of purifying the mind and the environment. It explains that purification does not mean the destruction of phenomena, but rather the realization of their true nature. It discusses the purification of the six sense bases, the purification of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and the purification of the field of merit. It teaches that when the mind is purified, all external circumstances naturally become conducive to practice. This chapter encourages the practitioner to maintain a pure heart in all activities. [End of Sixth Chapter] Ninth, the seventh part of the commentary: The seventh chapter is the Chapter on the Attainment of the Dharma. It describes the final stage of the path, the attainment of Buddhahood. It explains that the attainment of Buddhahood is not the acquisition of something new, but the full manifestation of what was already present within. It details the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. It emphasizes that a Buddha is one who has realized the equality of all beings and acts for their benefit without discrimination. This chapter inspires practitioners to aspire to the supreme goal of universal liberation. [End of Seventh Chapter] Tenth, the eighth part of the commentary: The eighth chapter is the Chapter on the Manifestation of the Dharma. It explains how a Buddha manifests in the world to teach the Dharma. It discusses the various types of emanations and the different ways in which the Buddha appears to different beings. It highlights the Buddha’s skillful means in adapting his teachings to the needs of his audience. It concludes by affirming that the ultimate purpose of all these manifestations is to lead sentient beings to the realization of the Mahāyāna truth. [End of Eighth Chapter] In summary, the *Mahāyāna-samparigraha-śāstra* is a comprehensive exposition of the Mahāyāna doctrine. It covers the fundamental nature of reality, the meaning of the teachings, the characteristics of phenomena, the methods of practice, the obstacles to be overcome, the process of purification, the attainment of the fruit, and the manifestation of the Dharma in the world. By studying this treatise, one gains a thorough understanding of the path to enlightenment and is able to apply it effectively in one’s own life. It is a work of enduring value for all seekers of truth. [End of Translation]
